structure.title: II. Historical Background (A. Inheritance in Ancien Regime France; B. 1793 Inheritance Reforms)
III. Data (A. Inheritance rules atlas; B. Henry database; C. Geni database)
IV. Empirical Strategy (A. DD specification; B. Identifying assumptions)
V.C Spatial RD-DD with Crowdsourced Genealogies
VI. Mechanisms (A. Land Fragmentation; B. Women's Bargaining Power)
VII. Conclusion and Data Availability statement

observations.statement: States a baseline difference-in-differences specification interacting a pre-1793 inheritance-system indicator with a post-reform fertile-cohort indicator, with cohort and municipality fixed effects, and names the coefficient as capturing the reform's combined effect on fertility.

Names a second design, a spatial regression-discontinuity difference-in-differences (RD-DD), comparing women born on opposite sides of historical judicial-district borders with different inheritance rules, before and after the reform harmonized rules across the border.

States that the DD identifying assumption is that fertility would have followed the same trend across areas with different prereform inheritance systems absent the reform, and supports this with cohort-level trend plots and an event-study specification.

Discusses the threat that local economic conditions could have evolved differently across areas with different prereform inheritance systems, and states that this motivates an extended specification allowing flexible, municipality-specific trends along economic, religious, political, and economic-geography characteristics.

Names the Enquete Louis Henry as the main individual-level fertility source, describes it as built by the family-reconstitution method linking birth, marriage and death records, and states the unit of observation is the individual woman within a birth cohort and municipality.

Names crowdsourced online genealogies from a commercial genealogy website as a second fertility source, and describes reconstructing individual fertility from family links in user-submitted profiles, geocoded and matched to a gazetteer for birth locations.
States the baseline Henry-database sample is women born across the eighteenth century, chosen to give a mix of cohorts that were and were not of fertile age at the time of the 1793 reform.

Reports dropping a small number of municipalities from the Henry database's nominative sample, justifying each exclusion by name (one that was outside France's 1789 territory, one with very few observations).

Describes applying a horizontal sample restriction to the crowdsourced genealogy data, following a cited prior method, keeping a profile only if a preceding generation has more than one recorded offspring, to correct a known bias toward overrepresenting single-child families in user-submitted genealogies.

Defines completed fertility as net fertility, counting only children who survived to a stated childhood age, and separately reports the same measure computed only among mothers and an indicator for childlessness within marriage.

Defines the treatment indicator at the municipality level as areas with prereform inegalitarian inheritance rules (impartible and/or excluding women), interacted with an indicator for cohorts of fertile age after the reform, and defines the reproductive span used to construct the exposure indicator, testing alternative span definitions as robustness.
Defines the RD running variable as the geographic distance from a woman's birth municipality to the nearest inheritance-system border, signed by which side of the border the location falls on.
States that municipality-level distance variables used as flexible-trend controls are entered in a log(1+distance) transformation, and that wheat-price series are entered in logs.
observations.locator: Section IV.B, footnote on flexible-trend controls

observations.statement: Constructs a religiosity index from the share of marriages occurring during Lent and Advent in the Henry-database marriage dates, reasoning that the Catholic Church did not marry couples in these periods while civil marriage could occur year-round, so the share proxies local secularization.

Reports cohort and municipality fixed effects as table rows in the baseline DD table and adds individual-level controls (literacy, form-accuracy category, parental survival at marriage) across successive columns of the same table.
Reports observation counts and adjusted R-squared for every column across the DD and flexible-trend tables.
States in table notes that standard errors are clustered by municipality for the DD tables and by municipality for the RD-DD tables, with standard errors shown in parentheses beneath coefficients.

Reports the mean of the dependent variable as a table row for the spatial RD-DD estimates, allowing readers to translate the reported discontinuity into a proportional change without the paper itself stating that percentage in the row.
Clusters standard errors at the municipality level in the baseline DD specification, the level at which the prereform inheritance-system treatment is assigned.

Addresses the small number of municipality clusters in the Henry-database sample by reporting a wild-bootstrap procedure from a cited paper as an alternative inference method alongside the baseline standard errors.

Reports Conley-type spatially adjusted standard errors under several distance cutoffs for both the DD and RD-DD estimates, to allow for spatial correlation in the error term beyond municipality clustering.
observations.locator: Section IV.A; Section V.B 'Spatially adjusted errors'; Section V.C robustness

observations.statement: Reports a balance table comparing prereform individual- and municipality-level characteristics across egalitarian and inegalitarian inheritance areas, covering mortality, family-survival, literacy, price, density, religiosity, distance, and soil/terrain variables, to argue the two groups are otherwise comparable.

Reports a figure plotting average completed fertility by birth cohort separately for areas with different prereform inheritance rules, with local polynomial trend lines and confidence bands split around the last prereform cohort.

Reports an event-study figure with cohort-bin interaction coefficients and confidence intervals relative to an omitted cohort, used to test for a differential prereform fertility trend between treated and control municipalities.

Reports a placebo test restricted to cohorts whose entire reproductive span occurred before the reform, estimating the same specification with a placebo reform date and placing the table in the online appendix.

Reports that RD-DD estimates are checked across a range of bandwidths narrower and wider than the mean-squared-error optimal choice for both linear and quadratic polynomial specifications, with the sensitivity figure placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section V.C, robustness discussion (Figure E3, appendix)

observations.statement: Reports a permutation-test exercise reshuffling the prereform inheritance-system assignment across municipalities many times to build a placebo distribution of the treatment coefficient, comparing the baseline estimate's rank against this distribution, with results placed in an appendix figure.
Reports a jackknife exercise sequentially omitting each municipality from the Henry-database sample to check that no single municipality drives the DD estimates, with results in an appendix figure.
observations.locator: Section V.B, 'Sensitivity to outliers' (Figure D2, appendix)

observations.statement: Reports robustness to alternative sample restrictions, alternative reproductive-span cutoffs defining exposure, and alternative definitions of the treatment and control groups based separately on the partibility and women's-inheritance dimensions of the reform, with detailed tables in an appendix.
observations.locator: Section V.B, 'Alternative sample, treatment, and control group' (Tables D2-D4, appendix)

observations.statement: Reports robustness to restricting the Henry-database sample to women observed alive at the end of their reproductive span and to including municipality-specific mortality trends, addressing concerns that migration or differential mortality bias the family-reconstitution estimates.
observations.locator: Section V.B, 'Migration and mortality' (Table D5, appendix)

observations.statement: Reports robustness to adding interactions between soil texture, terrain ruggedness and cohort fixed effects, and to excluding a few municipalities with extreme terrain-ruggedness values, with results in an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section V.B, 'Soil, climate, and terrain characteristics' (Tables D7-D8, appendix)

observations.statement: Reports a heterogeneity specification interacting the reform-exposure variable with indicators for soil texture and terrain ruggedness, motivated by predictions of a stated theoretical model linking farm size to land-fragmentation incentives, and reports a formal test of the difference between the two interacted coefficients.

Reports that the same soil-based heterogeneity pattern is checked using four finer soil-texture categories and using the completed-fertility-of-mothers and childlessness outcomes, and replicated using the RD-DD design and database, with these extensions placed in appendix tables.

Presents qualitative evidence for the land-fragmentation mechanism drawn from statements by contemporary legislators and observers during the debate over the 1793 reform, and from cited historical case studies of land division.

Digitizes cadastral parcel records for a subset of municipalities under different prereform inheritance rules to measure land-parcel fragmentation directly, describing this as a source not previously used by economists for this purpose, and reports its association with prereform inheritance rules.
observations.locator: Section VI.A, 'Quantitative evidence from cadastre data'

observations.statement: Describes a theoretical model in which households under a subsistence land-input threshold limit fertility to avoid falling below that threshold when land must be divided among heirs, used to derive a testable heterogeneity prediction that is then taken to the data rather than estimated structurally.
observations.locator: Section VI.A, 'Heterogeneity analysis' (model detailed in online appendix G)

observations.statement: Interprets the main DD coefficient by expressing it as a proportional reduction relative to the sample average level of the outcome in treated areas before the reform.

Compares the estimated reform effect on fertility to the prereform fertility gap between egalitarian and inegalitarian inheritance areas reported in the balance table, arguing the two magnitudes are similar as a form of internal magnitude check.

Constructs a counterfactual exercise using the estimated flexible-trend specification to predict individual fertility absent the reform, then compares aggregate observed and counterfactual average fertility across two defined phases of France's demographic transition to attribute a share of the aggregate decline to the reform.
observations.locator: Section V.A, 'Implications for the demographic transition'

observations.statement: Reports a formal test of the equality of the interacted coefficients for areas favoring large versus small farms in the heterogeneity table, discussing whether the difference is statistically distinguishable across specifications rather than only comparing point estimates.

States explicitly that the ideal experiment to separate the land-fragmentation and women's-bargaining-power mechanisms is infeasible, because extending inheritance rights to women mechanically changes the number of heirs at the same time, so the two channels cannot be cleanly isolated with this design.
observations.locator: Section I, mechanisms discussion; Section VI.B

observations.statement: States explicitly that the paper does not claim the French Revolution was the only cause of France's fertility transition, noting other forces limiting fertility were already present beforehand.

Acknowledges that the crowdsourced genealogy database has lower data quality than the family-reconstitution database, while noting it offers broader geographic coverage, framing this as a trade-off rather than treating one source as strictly superior.
Presents the pretrends check as a coefficient plot over cohort bins with shaded confidence intervals rather than only as a table of coefficients.

Presents RD-DD evidence as binned scatter plots of residualized fertility against distance to the inheritance border, separately for pre- and post-reform subsamples, with a local polynomial fit line and confidence band, using a stated bin-selection rule from a cited method.
Presents the constructed inheritance-rules atlas and the geographic distribution of sampled observations as maps rather than only as tabulated shares.

Uses asterisks tied to conventional significance thresholds in every regression table, with a table note stating the clustering level and standard-error placement in parentheses beneath each coefficient.

Previews the direction and approximate size of the main DD and RD-DD fertility effects, and the counterfactual contribution to the demographic transition, within the introduction before the results are formally presented later in the paper.
Places the Data section before the Empirical Strategy section, describing the constructed inheritance atlas and both fertility databases before presenting the DD and RD-DD estimating equations.
Includes an explicit contributions paragraph in the introduction listing the paper's claimed contributions relative to the existing literature as a numbered sequence.

Places difference-in-differences robustness checks in their own labeled subsection distinct from the main results subsection, briefly summarizing each check in the main text and deferring full tables to the appendix.
States in a Data Availability section that code replicating the tables and figures is deposited in a named repository with a citable DOI.

States that the Data Availability section provides instructions for how to obtain the individual-level demographic data from the family-reconstitution survey and from the crowdsourced genealogy website, rather than redistributing the underlying individual-level data directly.

Describes the family-reconstitution database as built from parish and hospital records before the introduction of civil registers, and from civil registers afterward, characterizing it as an administrative/archival record linkage rather than a survey collected by the authors.

Discusses whether the finding could generalize beyond France, noting that similar egalitarian inheritance laws were later adopted across much of Europe partly through the spread of French revolutionary legal codes, and states as an open question whether this contributed to those countries' own demographic transitions.

States that the same type of inheritance reform is expected to reduce fertility specifically where landownership is fragmented, as in France, but not where landownership is concentrated, citing other countries as contrasting cases, tying external validity explicitly to the land-fragmentation mechanism.

gaps: No statement about sampling or survey weights anywhere in the main text; none of the reported specifications mention weighting.

No formal manipulation/density test (e.g. McCrary-style) for the RD running variable is reported in the read text; identification instead rests on the historically fixed, pre-existing judicial-district boundary and a covariate-smoothness balancing test.
No explicit multiple-hypothesis-testing adjustment is described despite many outcomes, subsamples, and specifications being reported across the DD and RD-DD analyses.

No preregistration, IRB approval, or participant-consent statement of any kind appears in the read text; the study uses historical archival and crowdsourced genealogical records, not living human subjects data collection.
No explicit statement of statistical software (e.g., Stata/R and version) appears in the main text.

The online appendixes A-H, referenced extensively for robustness tables, diagnostic figures, the formal model, and additional heterogeneity results, are a separate online document not included in this text extraction and were not read.
The introduction contains an explicit contributions paragraph but no separate roadmap paragraph laying out the order of the remaining sections.

reading.note: All 48 pages of the provided text were read in full: title/abstract through the Conclusion and Data Availability statement (pages 1-43), plus the reference list (pages 43-48) to confirm it is bibliography only and to locate the data-availability language. The paper's online appendixes A-H (cited throughout for detailed robustness tables, diagnostic figures, the formal land-fragmentation model, and supplementary heterogeneity results) are a separate document not included in this text extraction and were not read; their existence and general contents are recorded only as stated in the main text.
